title: Les Misérables
author: Victor Hugo
description: Hugo's Paris is the heart of the book, and he maps it street by street: the Gorbeau tenement on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital, the Luxembourg where Marius and Cosette fall in love, the convent of Petit-Picpus, the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie by Les Halles, and the sewers Valjean carries the wounded Marius through. The story reaches it from far off, though: from Digne in the Alps, from Montreuil-sur-Mer in the north, from the battlefield of Waterloo.

route.summary: Arrested with the silver he stole, the paroled convict Jean Valjean is dragged back to the bishop who fed him. Instead of accusing him, Monseigneur Bienvenu gives him the candlesticks too and buys his soul for God. The gift breaks Valjean open and sets the whole novel in motion; he carries the candlesticks for the rest of his life.
route.note: Hugo veils the town as “D——” throughout, but the see of the good Bishop Myriel is Digne, in the Alps of Provence; Hugo modelled Myriel on the real Bishop of Digne, Bienvenu de Miollis. The pin marks Digne-les-Bains, far south of the Paris setting.

route.summary: Valjean has vanished into a new life here as “Father Madeleine,” whose glass-bead factory has made the whole town prosper, and the grateful people push him into the mayor's chair. It is in his Montreuil that Fantine is driven from his own workshop into ruin, and that Inspector Javert first begins to circle the mayor he cannot place.
route.note: Hugo abbreviates the town as “M. sur M.” in these chapters but names it in full, Montreuil-sur-Mer, later in the book. The pin marks the walled town in the Pas-de-Calais, in northern France, well outside the Paris setting.

route.summary: Night has fallen on the lost battle, and the innkeeper Thénardier is out stripping the corpses. Robbing a half-buried officer, he accidentally drags the man free, and the officer, Colonel Pontmercy, believes himself rescued and swears to remember the name. Pontmercy is Marius's father; this squalid theft is the debt that later binds Marius to the Thénardiers.
route.note: The battlefield south of Waterloo is real and named throughout Hugo's long digression; he sets the robbery in the hollow road of Ohain, on the field itself. The pin marks the Lion's Mound, the monument raised over the battlefield in Belgium, far from the Paris setting.

route.summary: Marius, poor and adrift, has been watching the same white-haired old man and his daughter on a bench in the Luxembourg for months. On this warm morning she finally looks up, their eyes meet, and he is lost. The garden where they fall in love is real and unchanged, still spread below the Palais du Luxembourg on the Left Bank.

route.displayName: The barricade, Rue de la Chanvrerie
route.summary: This is the barricade the whole book has been climbing toward: a heap of overturned carts and torn-up paving in a dead-end street, the red flag raised over it, and a knot of doomed students under Enjolras waiting for an army. Marius comes here to die for love and country; Valjean comes to save him, and the sewers wait below.
route.note: The Rue de la Chanvrerie, where Hugo builds his barricade around the Corinthe wine-shop by Les Halles, was swept away when the Rue Rambuteau was cut through the quarter. The pin marks the neighbouring Rue Mondétour, named in the novel and still surviving, at the heart of the June 1832 rising near Saint-Merri.

route.summary: Carrying the unconscious Marius on his back, Valjean has dropped through a grating into the sewers to escape the soldiers hunting the barricade. Blind in the dark, wading the filth, feeling his way along the wall, he crosses Paris underground to bring his rival's body out alive. Hugo pauses the escape for a whole essay on the sewer as the city's conscience.
route.note: Hugo traces Valjean's underground march through named real sewers, but has him lose his way in the dark, so the exact route cannot be fixed. The pin marks the Musée des Égouts de Paris at the Pont de l'Alma, the working sewer where the city's underground is shown today.
